denomProfiles.tagline: Plain-living Anabaptists who keep a separate, disciplined community under the Ordnung.
coreDoctrines: Adult (believer's) baptism on confession of faith, usually between about 16 and 25, by pouring.
The Dordrecht Confession (1632) as the standard statement of faith.
Nonresistance: refusal of military service, lawsuits and the use of force.
Separation from the world (Romans 12:2) expressed through the unwritten Ordnung of each district.
Church discipline including the ban and social avoidance (Meidung) of unrepentant members.
Gelassenheit: yielding self-will to God and to the community.
focuses: Family, farm and small-business life within close-knit church districts.
Humility and simplicity in dress, transport and technology.
Mutual aid in place of commercial insurance and state welfare.
Forgiveness, notably shown after the Nickel Mines school shooting (2006).
practices: Three-hour Sunday worship every other week, held in members' homes or barns.
Slow unison singing from the Ausbund, a sixteenth-century Anabaptist hymnal.
Ministers, deacons and bishops chosen by lot from within the district, unpaid.
Communion twice a year, preceded by a council meeting and followed by foot washing.
Pennsylvania Dutch in daily life, High German Bible and hymns in worship.
Rumspringa, a period of youthful latitude before a young person chooses baptism.

influencedBy.name: Swiss Brethren
influencedBy.text: The Amish arose from a 1693 division among Swiss and Alsatian Anabaptists.

influencedBy.name: Mennonites
influencedBy.text: Shared Dutch Mennonite teaching, including the Dordrecht Confession and stricter shunning.

influencedBy.name: Martyrs Mirror
influencedBy.text: Thieleman van Braght's 1660 martyrology shapes Amish memory of persecution.

influenced.name: Amish Mennonites
influenced.text: Progressive Amish who in the 1860s-1870s merged mostly into Mennonite conferences.

influenced.name: Beachy Amish
influenced.text: A 1927 fellowship that allowed cars and electricity and adopted evangelical missions.

influenced.name: Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972)
influenced.text: A US Supreme Court ruling, won by Amish parents, that widened religious-liberty protection in schooling.

keyFigures.name: Jakob Ammann
keyFigures.role: Swiss elder whose call for stricter discipline led to the 1693 division

keyFigures.name: Hans Reist
keyFigures.role: Emmental Anabaptist leader who opposed Ammann on shunning

keyFigures.name: Menno Simons
keyFigures.role: Dutch Anabaptist leader whose teaching on the ban the Amish followed

members.note: About 400,000 people of all ages (adults and children) in the US and Canada, Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies, Amish Population 2024.

denomProfiles.tagline: Anabaptists who hold all property in common and live in rural colonies.
coreDoctrines: Community of goods (Gütergemeinschaft) as a mark of true discipleship, after Acts 2 and 4.
Believer's baptism and a disciplined church separated from the world.
Nonresistance and refusal of military service.
Peter Riedemann's Confession of Faith (Rechenschaft, 1540s) as the classic statement of belief.
Gelassenheit: surrender of self-will and private property to God and the community.
focuses: Colony life of roughly 60-160 people farming and manufacturing together.
Preserving the faith through a colony school, German school and church discipline.
Memory of martyrdom and migration recorded in the Great Chronicle.
Division into a new daughter colony when a colony grows too large.
practices: A short service every evening and a longer Sunday service, with sermons (Lehren) read from 16th-17th-century texts.
Communal meals in a common dining hall, men and women seated separately.
Ministers chosen by lot from candidates nominated by the colony.
Annual or near-annual communion at Easter.
Hutterisch (a Tyrolean-Carinthian German dialect) as the everyday language.
Plain, distinctive dress, though modern farm technology is widely used.

influencedBy.name: Anabaptism
influencedBy.text: Grew out of Anabaptist refugees gathered in Moravia from 1528.

influencedBy.name: Acts 2 and 4
influencedBy.text: The early Jerusalem church's shared goods is the scriptural model.

influencedBy.name: Tyrolean Anabaptism
influencedBy.text: Jakob Hutter organised Tyrolean refugees into disciplined communities in the 1530s.

influenced.name: Bruderhof
influenced.text: Eberhard Arnold's community (1920) united with the Hutterites in 1930; relations have since been broken and restored more than once.

influenced.name: Christian communal movements
influenced.text: A long-lived model studied by later intentional communities.

keyFigures.name: Jakob Hutter
keyFigures.role: Tyrolean leader and organiser, burned at Innsbruck in 1536

keyFigures.name: Peter Riedemann
keyFigures.role: Author of the Hutterite Confession of Faith

keyFigures.name: Andreas Ehrenpreis
keyFigures.role: Seventeenth-century elder who preserved community through war and persecution

keyFigures.name: Michael Waldner
keyFigures.role: Restored community of goods in Ukraine in 1859; the Schmiedeleut descend from him

denomProfiles.tagline: Pietist-Anabaptist peace church known for love feasts, simplicity and service.
coreDoctrines: "No force in religion" and "no creed but the New Testament": confessions are not imposed.
Believer's baptism by trine (threefold, forward) immersion.
Nonviolence: a historic peace church alongside Mennonites and Quakers.
Discipleship in community, discerning Scripture together.
Simplicity of life and nonconformity to the world.
focuses: Relief and development work: Brethren Service and the Heifer Project (Dan West, 1944).
Peacemaking and conscientious objection, including Civilian Public Service in the Second World War.
Congregational life and mutual care.
Continuing to work, by Annual Conference, through disagreements over sexuality, which led to departures around 2021.
practices: The love feast: self-examination, foot washing, a fellowship meal, then bread and cup.
Anointing of the sick with oil (James 5).
Annual Conference as the highest decision-making body; districts and congregations below it.
Women licensed to preach from 1922 and given full ordination from 1958.
Hymn-centred, mostly non-liturgical Sunday worship.

influencedBy.name: Radical Pietism
influencedBy.text: Ernst Christoph Hochmann von Hochenau and other Radical Pietists shaped the founders.

influencedBy.name: Anabaptism
influencedBy.text: Mennonite practice convinced Mack's circle of believer's baptism and nonresistance.

influencedBy.name: Mennonites
influencedBy.text: Neighbours and partners in Pennsylvania and in peace witness.

influenced.name: Old German Baptist Brethren
influenced.text: The conservative wing that separated in 1881.

influenced.name: The Brethren Church (Ashland)
influenced.text: Progressive wing that separated in 1883.

influenced.name: Grace Brethren
influenced.text: A further division of the Brethren Church in 1939.

influenced.name: Church of North India
influenced.text: Brethren mission churches in Gujarat joined the CNI in 1970.

keyFigures.name: Alexander Mack
keyFigures.role: Founder; led the eight first baptisms at Schwarzenau in 1708

keyFigures.name: Christopher Sauer
keyFigures.role: Germantown printer of the first European-language Bible in America (1743)

keyFigures.name: Alexander Mack Jr.
keyFigures.role: Elder and writer in colonial Germantown

keyFigures.name: Dan West
keyFigures.role: Founder of the Heifer Project

denomProfiles.inIndia: Brethren missionaries began work at Bulsar (Valsad), Gujarat, in 1895; most of these churches entered the Church of North India in 1970, while a minority continued separately as the First District Church of the Brethren.

denomProfiles.tagline: Anabaptist, Pietist and Wesleyan streams joined in one evangelical peace church.
coreDoctrines: Personal conversion and new birth, from its Pietist roots.
Believer's baptism by trine immersion.
Wesleyan-holiness teaching of sanctification, adopted in the early twentieth century.
Nonresistance and peacemaking from Anabaptist tradition.
Obedient discipleship within a caring church community.
focuses: Evangelism and church planting, especially in southern Africa and South Asia.
Peace and reconciliation ministries.
Higher education through Messiah University (founded 1909, Grantham, Pennsylvania).
Holding together Anabaptist, Pietist and Wesleyan emphases.
practices: Foot washing observed with the Lord's Supper.
Baptism by trine immersion.
General Conference with bishops (regional overseers) and local congregations.
Contemporary evangelical worship in many North American churches.
Membership in the Mennonite World Conference.

influencedBy.name: Mennonites
influencedBy.text: Founders included Mennonites of Lancaster County, Pennsylvania.

influencedBy.name: Pietism
influencedBy.text: Revival preaching, including that of the United Brethren, stressed a felt conversion.

influencedBy.name: Holiness movement
influencedBy.text: Second-blessing sanctification was adopted around 1910.

influencedBy.name: Evangelicalism
influencedBy.text: Joined the National Association of Evangelicals in 1949.

influenced.name: Brethren in Christ in Zimbabwe and Zambia
influenced.text: Missions from 1898 grew into churches now larger than the North American body.

influenced.name: Old Order River Brethren
influenced.text: Conservative groups that separated in the nineteenth century to keep older ways.

keyFigures.name: Jacob Engel
keyFigures.role: Early leader of the River Brethren in the 1770s-1780s

keyFigures.name: Frances Davidson
keyFigures.role: Pioneer missionary to Matopo, Southern Rhodesia (1898)

denomProfiles.inIndia: Brethren in Christ missionaries began work in Bihar in 1914, around Saharsa and Madhepura; the Indian church has since spread into Odisha and other states.

denomProfiles.tagline: Believer's baptism, gathered congregations and religious liberty for all.
coreDoctrines: The Bible as the final authority for faith and practice.
Baptism by immersion only for those who profess faith.
A regenerate church membership gathered in local, self-governing congregations.
The priesthood of all believers and soul liberty.
Religious freedom and the separation of church and state.
Two ordinances, baptism and the Lord's Supper, understood as obedience and witness.
focuses: Evangelism and world mission, from William Carey's Baptist Missionary Society (1792) onwards.
Preaching as the centre of worship.
Freedom of conscience and opposition to established churches.
Voluntary association of churches in unions and conventions.
practices: Immersion of believers, often in a baptistry in the church.
Lord's Supper monthly or quarterly, as a memorial.
Church meetings in which members vote on pastors and business.
Confessions (e.g. 1644, 1677/1689, the Baptist Faith and Message) used as guides, not creeds.
Associations and the Baptist World Alliance (1905) linking churches.

influencedBy.name: English Separatists
influencedBy.text: Smyth and Helwys began as Separatists seeking a pure gathered church.

influencedBy.name: Waterlander Mennonites
influencedBy.text: Contact in Amsterdam shaped early Baptist views of baptism and liberty.

influencedBy.name: Reformed theology
influencedBy.text: Particular Baptists adopted a Calvinist confession close to Westminster.

influenced.name: Evangelicalism
influenced.text: Baptists became one of the largest evangelical families.

influenced.name: Stone-Campbell Movement
influenced.text: The Campbells worked within Baptist associations between 1815 and 1830.

influenced.name: Seventh-day Adventists
influenced.text: Many early Adventists, including William Miller, were Baptists.

influenced.name: US Bill of Rights
influenced.text: Baptist campaigners such as John Leland and Isaac Backus pressed for religious liberty.

keyFigures.name: John Smyth
keyFigures.role: Founded the first Baptist church, Amsterdam 1609

keyFigures.name: Thomas Helwys
keyFigures.role: Brought the first Baptist church to England (1612) and pleaded for liberty of conscience

keyFigures.name: Roger Williams
keyFigures.role: Founded Providence and the first Baptist church in America (1638-39)

keyFigures.name: William Carey
keyFigures.role: Pioneer of modern Protestant missions in India

keyFigures.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
keyFigures.role: Baptist pastor and civil-rights leader

members.note: Approximate baptised membership of churches in the Baptist World Alliance's member bodies, as published by the BWA; the wider Baptist community, including children and non-BWA bodies, is larger.

denomProfiles.inIndia: Baptist churches are largest in North-East India: most Christians in Nagaland and many in Manipur, Meghalaya (Garo Hills) and southern Mizoram are Baptist, alongside older Telugu Baptist churches in Andhra Pradesh from the American Baptist mission and the Serampore legacy in Bengal.

denomProfiles.tagline: The first English Baptists, teaching that Christ died for all.
coreDoctrines: General atonement: Christ died for all people, not only the elect.
Believer's baptism (by immersion from the 1640s).
Liberty of conscience for all, including non-Christians (Helwys, 1612).
The Standard Confession (1660) and the Orthodox Creed (1679).
Laying on of hands for the newly baptised, taught as a principle in Hebrews 6 by many congregations.
focuses: A disciplined gathered church.
Religious toleration in Stuart England.
Evangelical revival in the New Connexion (1770) under Dan Taylor.
Mission in Orissa through the General Baptist Missionary Society (1816).
practices: Messengers serving several churches, and a General Assembly from the 1650s.
Plain worship; many early congregations opposed congregational hymn singing.
Lord's Supper as a memorial.
Church discipline exercised by the members.

influencedBy.name: English Separatists
influencedBy.text: Smyth's Gainsborough congregation emigrated to Amsterdam as Separatists.

influencedBy.name: Waterlander Mennonites
influencedBy.text: Mennonite views on free will and liberty influenced Smyth and Helwys.

influencedBy.name: Arminian theology
influencedBy.text: Shared the rejection of unconditional election associated with Jacobus Arminius.

influenced.name: Unitarianism
influenced.text: Many Old Connexion churches drifted into Unitarianism in the eighteenth century.

influenced.name: Free Will Baptists
influenced.text: American Arminian Baptists continue the General Baptist line.

influenced.name: Baptist Union of Great Britain
influenced.text: The New Connexion united with Particular Baptists in 1891.

keyFigures.name: John Smyth
keyFigures.role: Se-baptised and founded the first Baptist church (1609)

keyFigures.name: Thomas Helwys
keyFigures.role: Author of A Short Declaration of the Mistery of Iniquity (1612)

keyFigures.name: Thomas Grantham
keyFigures.role: Leading seventeenth-century General Baptist writer and messenger

keyFigures.name: Dan Taylor
keyFigures.role: Founder of the evangelical New Connexion (1770)

denomProfiles.inIndia: The New Connexion's General Baptist Missionary Society sent missionaries to Cuttack, Orissa (Odisha), from 1822; the churches it founded later joined the Church of North India (1970).

denomProfiles.tagline: Calvinistic Baptists of the London Confessions and the modern missionary movement.
coreDoctrines: Particular (definite) redemption: Christ died effectually for the elect.
Reformed teaching on grace and the sovereignty of God.
Believer's baptism by immersion, practised from about 1641.
The First (1644) and Second (1677, reissued 1689) London Confessions.
Covenant theology adapted to a gathered church of believers.
focuses: Preaching and doctrinal teaching.
World mission, after Andrew Fuller rebutted hyper-Calvinism.
Liberty of conscience under the Restoration and after.
Debate between strict and open communion.
practices: Immersion of professing believers.
Congregational government with elders and deacons.
Hymn singing, defended by Benjamin Keach against much opposition in the 1690s.
Associations of churches meeting regularly for counsel.

influencedBy.name: Independents
influencedBy.text: Emerged from the Jacob-Lathrop-Jessey church in London in the 1630s.

influencedBy.name: Westminster Confession
influencedBy.text: The Second London Confession closely follows Westminster and Savoy.

influencedBy.name: Puritanism
influencedBy.text: Shared Puritan piety and preaching.

influenced.name: Baptist Missionary Society
influenced.text: Founded at Kettering in 1792, sending William Carey to India.

influenced.name: Philadelphia Baptist Association
influenced.text: Its 1742 Philadelphia Confession carried the London Confession to America.

influenced.name: Strict and Reformed Baptists
influenced.text: Modern Calvinistic Baptists continue the 1689 Confession.

influenced.name: Southern Baptists
influenced.text: Early Southern Baptists drew on this Calvinist heritage.

keyFigures.name: William Kiffin
keyFigures.role: London merchant and pastor, signatory of the 1644 Confession

keyFigures.name: Benjamin Keach
keyFigures.role: Pastor and catechist who championed hymn singing

keyFigures.name: John Gill
keyFigures.role: Eighteenth-century theologian and commentator

keyFigures.name: Andrew Fuller
keyFigures.role: Author of The Gospel Worthy of All Acceptation (1785)

keyFigures.name: Charles Haddon Spurgeon
keyFigures.role: Victorian preacher at the Metropolitan Tabernacle

denomProfiles.inIndia: William Carey reached Bengal in 1793; the Serampore mission (from 1800) of Carey, Marshman and Ward translated the Bible into many Indian languages and founded Serampore College (1818). BMS-related churches in Bengal and Odisha largely joined the Church of North India in 1970.

denomProfiles.tagline: America's largest Protestant denomination, built on missions and cooperative giving.
coreDoctrines: The Baptist Faith and Message (1925, revised 1963 and 2000) as its confession.
Biblical inerrancy, affirmed in the 2000 revision.
Salvation by grace through personal faith in Christ.
Local church autonomy and believer's baptism by immersion.
Complementarian teaching: the office of pastor is limited to men (2000).
focuses: Evangelism and church planting through the North American Mission Board.
Foreign missions through the International Mission Board.
Funding through the Cooperative Program (1925).
Theological education in six seminaries.
Public engagement on religious liberty and moral issues via the Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission.
practices: Annual meeting of messengers sent by cooperating churches.
Revival-style invitations and altar calls in many churches.
Sunday School and Vacation Bible School.
Lottie Moon Christmas Offering for international missions.
Lord's Supper as a memorial, usually quarterly or monthly.

influencedBy.name: Baptist Churches
influencedBy.text: Separated from the national Baptist mission societies in 1845.

influencedBy.name: Particular Baptists
influencedBy.text: Early Southern Baptist confessions were Calvinistic.

influencedBy.name: Evangelicalism
influencedBy.text: Revivalism and later the conservative evangelical movement shaped its identity.

influenced.name: Cooperative Baptist Fellowship
influenced.text: Moderates formed the CBF (1991) after the conservative resurgence.

influenced.name: Baptist missions worldwide
influenced.text: Its missionaries planted many national conventions, including in Nigeria and Brazil.

influenced.name: Brazilian Baptist Convention
influenced.text: Grew from Southern Baptist missionaries in Brazil from 1881.

keyFigures.name: William Bullein Johnson
keyFigures.role: First president (1845)

keyFigures.name: Lottie Moon
keyFigures.role: Missionary to China, namesake of the mission offering

keyFigures.name: E. Y. Mullins
keyFigures.role: Theologian and seminary president; framed soul competency

keyFigures.name: Adrian Rogers
keyFigures.role: Pastor whose 1979 election began the conservative resurgence

keyFigures.name: Billy Graham
keyFigures.role: Southern Baptist evangelist

members.note: Reported membership in the 2024 Annual Church Profile compiled by Lifeway Research; weekly attendance is far lower.

denomProfiles.inIndia: Southern Baptist missionaries have worked in India mainly through medical and church-planting ministries; Bangalore Baptist Hospital, opened in 1973, is the best-known institution.

denomProfiles.tagline: The largest African American denomination: church, school and civil-rights base.
coreDoctrines: Evangelical Baptist faith: salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as ordinances.
Autonomy of the local church within a voluntary national convention.
Scripture as the rule of faith, broadly following the New Hampshire Confession (1833).
focuses: Black self-help, education and economic uplift.
Foreign missions in Africa and the Caribbean.
Publishing through its own Sunday School Publishing Board.
Civil rights and social justice, debated sharply in the 1950s-1960s.
practices: Expressive preaching, gospel music and call-and-response worship.
Annual session of messengers and a strong presidency.
Women's missionary and educational work (Woman's Convention, 1900).
Communion monthly in many churches, often on the first Sunday.

influencedBy.name: Baptist Churches
influencedBy.text: Formed from Black Baptist conventions in 1895.

influencedBy.name: The Black church tradition
influencedBy.text: Rooted in independent Black congregations since the late eighteenth century.

influencedBy.name: African American freedom struggle
influencedBy.text: Emancipation and Reconstruction shaped its mission of uplift.

influenced.name: National Baptist Convention of America
influenced.text: Separated in 1915 after a dispute over the publishing house.

influenced.name: Progressive National Baptist Convention
influenced.text: Formed in 1961 by Baptists, including King, who backed direct civil-rights action.

influenced.name: Civil-rights movement
influenced.text: Many leaders of the movement were National Baptist pastors.

keyFigures.name: Elias Camp Morris
keyFigures.role: First president (1895-1922)

keyFigures.name: Nannie Helen Burroughs
keyFigures.role: Leader of the Woman's Convention and educator

keyFigures.name: Joseph H. Jackson
keyFigures.role: President 1953-1982, who opposed civil-disobedience tactics

keyFigures.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
keyFigures.role: Raised in a National Baptist church; later Progressive

denomProfiles.tagline: Mainline, multi-ethnic Baptists rooted in the first national mission societies.
coreDoctrines: Believer's baptism and the Lord's Supper as ordinances.
Soul liberty and freedom of conscience; no binding creed.
Scripture as the authoritative guide, interpreted in community.
Local church autonomy within regional and national bodies.
focuses: Home and foreign missions, from the Triennial Convention (1814).
Racial and ethnic diversity in its congregations.
Ecumenism: a member of the National Council of Churches and the World Council of Churches.
Social justice, from Walter Rauschenbusch's Social Gospel onward.
practices: Regions and a Biennial Mission Summit linking autonomous churches.
Ordination of women as pastors.
Varied worship, from traditional to contemporary and ethnic-language congregations.
Lord's Supper commonly monthly.

influencedBy.name: Baptist Churches
influencedBy.text: Heirs of the northern Baptist mission societies after the 1845 split.

influencedBy.name: Social Gospel
influencedBy.text: Rauschenbusch, of Rochester Seminary, shaped its social witness.

influencedBy.name: Liberal theology
influencedBy.text: The University of Chicago Divinity School and modernist Baptists shaped its early-20th-century debates.

influenced.name: Baptist missions in Asia
influenced.text: Missions to Burma (Judson, 1813), North-East India and Andhra planted large Baptist churches.

influenced.name: Conservative Baptist Association
influenced.text: Formed (1947) by conservatives who left during fundamentalist-modernist disputes.

influenced.name: General Association of Regular Baptist Churches
influenced.text: Fundamentalist Baptists who withdrew in 1932.

keyFigures.name: Adoniram and Ann Hasseltine Judson
keyFigures.role: Missionaries to Burma whose call prompted the Triennial Convention

keyFigures.name: Luther Rice
keyFigures.role: Organiser of national Baptist support for missions

keyFigures.name: Walter Rauschenbusch
keyFigures.role: Social Gospel theologian

keyFigures.name: Harry Emerson Fosdick
keyFigures.role: Liberal preacher of Riverside Church

denomProfiles.inIndia: American Baptist missionaries reached Assam in 1836 and the Naga Hills from 1872, and began the Telugu mission at Nellore (1840), where thousands were baptised at Ongole in 1878; the Council of Baptist Churches in North East India and Telugu Baptist bodies grew from this work.

denomProfiles.tagline: Baptists who keep Saturday, the seventh day, as the Sabbath.
coreDoctrines: The seventh day (Saturday) is the biblical Sabbath to be kept holy.
Believer's baptism by immersion.
Salvation by grace through faith; Sabbath-keeping as obedience, not a means of salvation.
Congregational autonomy and liberty of conscience.
focuses: Sabbath witness to other Christians.
Small, close-knit congregations.
Missions in Africa, Asia and Latin America through a world federation.
practices: Worship on Saturday, the Sabbath beginning at sunset on Friday.
General Conference of North America (1802) linking churches, now based at Janesville, Wisconsin.
Lord's Supper as a memorial.
Seventh Day Baptist World Federation linking national conferences.

influencedBy.name: English Baptists
influencedBy.text: Sabbatarian congregations appeared among English Baptists in the 1650s (Mill Yard, London).

influencedBy.name: Puritan Sabbatarianism
influencedBy.text: Strict Puritan Sabbath teaching led some to adopt the seventh day.

influenced.name: Seventh-day Adventists
influenced.text: Rachel Oakes Preston, a Seventh Day Baptist, introduced the Sabbath to Adventists at Washington, New Hampshire, in 1844.

influenced.name: Church of God (Seventh Day)
influenced.text: Shared Sabbatarian convictions in the nineteenth century.

keyFigures.name: Francis Bampfield
keyFigures.role: Seventeenth-century Sabbatarian pastor in London, died in Newgate prison

keyFigures.name: Stephen Mumford
keyFigures.role: Brought Sabbatarian views to Newport, Rhode Island, in 1664

keyFigures.name: Rachel Oakes Preston
keyFigures.role: Seventh Day Baptist who brought Sabbath-keeping to the Adventists

denomProfiles.tagline: Arminian Baptists: free grace for all, believers' freedom, and foot washing.
coreDoctrines: General atonement: Christ died for all people.
Free will: grace enables every person to accept or reject salvation.
Conditional security: a believer can fall away through persistent unbelief.
Believer's baptism by immersion.
The Treatise of the Faith and Practices of the National Association (1935).
focuses: Evangelism and revival in the American South and Midwest.
Home and foreign missions.
Bible-college education (Welch College, Nashville, 1942).
Holy living and conservative evangelical ethics.
practices: Three ordinances: baptism, the Lord's Supper and the washing of the saints' feet.
Congregational government with associations and a National Association (1935).
Revival meetings and gospel singing.
Pastors are men in most churches.

influencedBy.name: General Baptists
influencedBy.text: Paul Palmer's 1727 North Carolina church drew on English General Baptist teaching.

influencedBy.name: New Light revivalism
influencedBy.text: Benjamin Randall was converted under George Whitefield's preaching in 1770.

influencedBy.name: Arminian theology
influencedBy.text: Shares the Arminian view of grace and free will.

influenced.name: Northern Baptist Convention
influenced.text: Most northern (Randall) Free Baptists merged with Northern Baptists in 1911.

influenced.name: Pentecostal Free Will Baptist Church
influenced.text: Free Will Baptists in North Carolina who accepted Pentecostal teaching after 1907.

keyFigures.name: Paul Palmer
keyFigures.role: Organised the first southern Free Will Baptist church (1727)

keyFigures.name: Benjamin Randall
keyFigures.role: Founded the northern Freewill Baptist movement at New Durham, New Hampshire (1780)

denomProfiles.inIndia: The northern Freewill Baptists ran a mission at Balasore and Midnapore in Odisha and Bengal from 1836; after the 1911 merger it passed to the American Baptists.

denomProfiles.tagline: One of the world's largest Baptist conventions, rooted in Yorubaland since 1850.
coreDoctrines: Evangelical Baptist faith: salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
Authority of Scripture and local church autonomy.
A confession in the Southern Baptist tradition.
focuses: Evangelism and church planting across Nigeria and in neighbouring countries.
Education: schools, the Nigerian Baptist Theological Seminary at Ogbomoso and Bowen University (Iwo, 2001).
Medical work, including the Baptist hospital at Ogbomoso.
Christian witness in a religiously plural nation, including in northern states.
practices: Worship in Yoruba, English and many other Nigerian languages.
Associations and conferences under a national convention based at Ibadan.
Strong women's and youth organisations.
Lively music and prayer meetings alongside Baptist order.

influencedBy.name: Southern Baptist Convention
influencedBy.text: Thomas Jefferson Bowen began Southern Baptist work in Yorubaland in 1850.

influencedBy.name: Yoruba Christian leadership
influencedBy.text: Nigerian Baptists sustained the work when missionaries withdrew during the American Civil War.

influencedBy.name: African church movement
influencedBy.text: The 1888 Native Baptist secession pressed for African leadership.

influenced.name: Baptist work in West Africa
influenced.text: Nigerian Baptists send missionaries to neighbouring countries and beyond.

influenced.name: Baptist World Alliance
influenced.text: Among the largest member bodies of the BWA.

keyFigures.name: Thomas Jefferson Bowen
keyFigures.role: Pioneer Southern Baptist missionary in Yorubaland from 1850

keyFigures.name: Mojola Agbebi
keyFigures.role: Lagos Baptist leader of the 1888 Native Baptist church and of African church independence

denomProfiles.tagline: Brazil's leading historic Baptist body, planted from Salvador in 1882.
coreDoctrines: Evangelical Baptist faith: salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
Believer's baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
Authority of Scripture and local church autonomy.
Religious liberty and separation of church and state.
focuses: Evangelism and church planting across Brazil.
National and world missions boards sending Brazilian missionaries abroad.
Theological education, including the South Brazil Baptist Theological Seminary in Rio de Janeiro (1908).
Social and educational work.
practices: Congregational government with state conventions and a national assembly.
Hymnody from the Cantor Cristão, the Brazilian Baptist hymnal.
Worship styles ranging from traditional to contemporary.
Lord's Supper as a memorial, often monthly.

denomProfiles.tagline: Wesley's revival: grace for all, warm-hearted faith and holy living.
coreDoctrines: Prevenient grace: God's grace goes before every person, enabling a free response.
Justification by faith and the witness of the Spirit (assurance).
Christian perfection or entire sanctification: love made perfect in this life.
Universal offer of salvation, against unconditional predestination.
Doctrinal standards in Wesley's Sermons, Notes on the New Testament and the Articles of Religion.
Scripture as primary, read with tradition, reason and experience (the "Wesleyan quadrilateral", Albert Outler's term).
focuses: Evangelism and preaching to the poor, outdoors if need be.
Social holiness: schools, hospitals, temperance and anti-slavery.
Small-group discipleship in class meetings and bands.
Sung theology through Charles Wesley's hymns.
practices: A connexion of societies governed by Conference, with ministers stationed by appointment.
Infant baptism and the Lord's Supper, Wesley urging "constant communion".
Covenant service, love feasts and watchnight services.
Itinerant ministry and local (lay) preachers.
Hymn singing at the centre of worship.

influencedBy.name: Moravians

influencedBy.name: Holy living writers

influencedBy.name: Arminianism

influenced.name: Holiness movement

denomProfiles.inIndia: British Wesleyans worked in Madras and the Tamil country from 1817 and their churches joined the Church of South India in 1947; American Methodist Episcopal work from Bareilly (William Butler, 1856) grew into the Methodist Church in India, autonomous since 1981.

denomProfiles.tagline: Nineteenth-century revival of Wesley's call to entire sanctification.
coreDoctrines: Entire sanctification as a second, instantaneous work of grace after conversion.
Heart purity and perfect love made possible by the Holy Spirit.
Phoebe Palmer's "altar theology": consecrate all and claim the promise by faith.
Salvation offered to all, received by faith.
Strict personal ethics and separation from worldliness.
focuses: Camp meetings and revivals.
Holiness literature, periodicals and Bible schools.
Ministry to the urban poor and rescue missions.
Women's preaching, defended by Palmer in Promise of the Father (1859).
practices: National Camp Meeting Association for the Promotion of Holiness (Vineland, New Jersey, 1867).
Testimony meetings and altar calls for sanctification.
Plain dress and abstinence from alcohol and tobacco in many groups.
Simple, revivalist worship with gospel songs.

denomProfiles.inIndia: Holiness bodies including the Salvation Army, Free Methodists, Nazarenes and the Church of God (Anderson) have Indian churches; Union Biblical Seminary, founded at Yavatmal in 1938 by a Free Methodist missionary and now at Pune, has trained many Indian evangelical leaders.

denomProfiles.tagline: A holiness church organised as an army, joining evangelism with social service.
coreDoctrines: Eleven articles of faith, evangelical and Wesleyan in character.
Salvation by grace through faith, offered to all.
Entire sanctification: holiness of heart and life.
Sacraments not observed outwardly since 1883; the life of grace is held to be possible without them.
The Trinity, the full deity and humanity of Christ, and the authority of Scripture.
focuses: Evangelism among the poor, the homeless and the excluded.
Social service: shelters, rehabilitation, disaster relief and anti-trafficking work.
Total abstinence from alcohol and non-medical drugs for soldiers.
Equal ministry of women and men as officers from the start.
practices: Uniforms, ranks, corps (local churches) and officers (ordained ministers).
Soldiers enrolled by signing the Soldier's Covenant.
Brass bands, songsters and open-air meetings.
The mercy seat, where people kneel to pray for salvation or holiness.
An international General elected by the High Council (since 1929).

influenced.name: Social welfare and reform

influenced.name: Urban missions

denomProfiles.tagline: The first independent Black denomination in the US, born of protest at segregation.
coreDoctrines: Methodist doctrine in the Articles of Religion inherited from Wesley.
Salvation by grace through faith for all, and growth in holiness.
Human equality before God: "God our Father, Christ our Redeemer, Man our Brother".
Infant and adult baptism and the Lord's Supper as sacraments.
focuses: Black self-determination and dignity in church and society.
Education: Wilberforce University (bought by the church in 1863) and other colleges.
Civil rights and community uplift.
Missions in Africa and the Caribbean.
practices: Episcopal government with bishops, General Conference every four years and districts.
Methodist liturgy with spirited Black preaching and music.
Monthly communion in many congregations.
Publishing through the Christian Recorder (from 1852).
Women ordained; Vashti McKenzie became the first woman bishop in 2000.

coreDoctrines: Methodist doctrine in the Articles of Religion.
Salvation by grace through faith and growth in holiness.
Human equality and freedom as implications of the gospel.
Infant and adult baptism and the Lord's Supper as sacraments.
focuses: Abolition and the Underground Railroad in the nineteenth century.
Education through Livingstone College (Salisbury, North Carolina, 1879).
Civil rights and social justice.
Missions in West Africa (Liberia, Ghana, Nigeria) and the Caribbean.
practices: Episcopal government with bishops and a quadrennial General Conference.
Methodist worship with Black gospel preaching and music.
Publishing through the Star of Zion newspaper.
Early ordination of women: Julia Foote as deacon (1894) and Mary Small as elder (1898).

denomProfiles.tagline: Global connexional Methodism, re-shaped by disaffiliations and 2024 reforms.
coreDoctrines: Doctrinal standards: the Articles of Religion, the EUB Confession of Faith, Wesley's Sermons and Notes.
Prevenient, justifying and sanctifying grace.
Scripture as primary, illumined by tradition, experience and reason ("Our Theological Task", 1972).
Baptism and the Lord's Supper as sacraments, with an open table.
Social Principles (1972) setting out positions on society and ethics.
focuses: Mission and relief through the United Methodist Committee on Relief (UMCOR).
Social justice and public witness.
Education: many universities, seminaries and schools.
A worldwide church with rapid growth in Africa and the Philippines.
practices: General Conference, Council of Bishops and Judicial Council governing the connexion.
Clergy appointed by bishops to local churches.
Book of Discipline and the United Methodist Hymnal and Book of Worship.
Women given full clergy rights in 1956; Marjorie Matthews was the first woman bishop (1980).
In 2024 General Conference removed bans on gay clergy and same-sex weddings and approved regionalisation.

Salvation by grace through faith offered to all.
Scripture as the final authority.
Baptism and the Lord's Supper as sacraments.
Articles of Religion adapted from Methodism.

Opposition to slavery and to secret oath-bound societies, from its founding.
Holiness of life and simplicity.
World mission; most members today live outside North America.

Lay delegates with an equal voice to clergy in conference.
Infant and believer's baptism both accepted.
Women ordained as elders since 1974, after earlier evangelist and deacon roles.

denomProfiles.tagline: Abolitionist and holiness Methodists united in 1968; pioneers in women's ministry.
coreDoctrines: Entire sanctification as a work of grace after conversion.
Salvation by grace through faith offered to all.
Scripture as inspired and authoritative.
Baptism and the Lord's Supper as sacraments.
focuses: Holiness of life and evangelism.
Social justice, rooted in its abolitionist founding (1843).
Church multiplication in North America and abroad.
Higher education through Indiana Wesleyan, Houghton and other universities.
practices: General Conference with general superintendents and districts.
Women ordained since the nineteenth century.
Infant and believer's baptism both accepted.
Contemporary worship in many churches.

Salvation by grace through faith, available to all.
Scripture inerrant in all things relating to salvation.
Baptism (infant or believer) and the Lord's Supper as sacraments.
focuses: Holiness preaching and Christlike discipleship.
Global mission; most members now live outside the US.
Compassionate ministries to the poor.
Education through Nazarene universities and seminaries.
practices: General Assembly, general superintendents, districts and local churches.
